chapter_text:
CHAPTER 24 — NATIONAL INTEGRATION AND SECULARISM

Introduction

India is one of the most diverse countries in the world. Within its borders live people speaking hundreds of LANGUAGES, following many RELIGIONS, belonging to thousands of CASTES and tribes, eating different foods, wearing different clothes, celebrating different festivals. The Constitution recognises 22 SCHEDULED LANGUAGES, and there are MAJOR FAITHS — Hinduism (~80%), Islam (~14%), Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism, plus many tribal religions. Holding such a country together as ONE NATION is an extraordinary achievement — and a continuous challenge. The values that bind India together — NATIONAL INTEGRATION and SECULARISM — are the subject of this chapter.

24.1 WHAT IS NATIONAL INTEGRATION?

NATIONAL INTEGRATION is the feeling of ONENESS among all citizens of a country, transcending religion, caste, language, region, and other differences. It is not UNIFORMITY (everyone being the same) but UNITY IN DIVERSITY (different people sharing a common political and emotional bond as Indians).

Key FEATURES of national integration:
 - Shared political identity as INDIAN CITIZENS.
 - Loyalty to the CONSTITUTION and to the nation as a whole.
 - Sense of common HISTORY, culture and destiny.
 - Mutual RESPECT among different communities.
 - Willingness to ACT TOGETHER in the national interest, especially in times of crisis.
 - Acceptance of LEGITIMATE differences within a common framework.

National integration does NOT mean wiping out diversity. Indians can be proud Tamils, Bengalis, Punjabis, Christians, Muslims, Sikhs — and still be Indians first. The Preamble's promise of FRATERNITY 'assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation' captures this idea.

24.2 OBSTACLES TO NATIONAL INTEGRATION

India faces several obstacles:

(1) COMMUNALISM — religion-based politics and violence (studied in detail in Chapter 23). Major incidents — Partition, 1984, 1992-93, 2002 riots — have torn the social fabric.

(2) CASTEISM — discrimination, atrocities and political mobilisation on caste lines.

(3) REGIONALISM — anti-migrant 'sons-of-soil' movements; separatist demands; inter-state disputes over rivers and borders.

(4) LINGUISTIC TENSIONS — disputes over official languages; opposition to imposition of Hindi in non-Hindi states (especially Tamil Nadu); demands for new linguistic states.

(5) ECONOMIC DISPARITIES — uneven development across regions; concentration of wealth; tribal areas left behind.

(6) SEPARATIST MOVEMENTS — historical agitations in Punjab, J&K, the North-east, and Left-Wing Extremism in central tribal areas.

(7) EXTERNAL FORCES — neighbouring countries sometimes support insurgents; terrorist groups operating across borders.

24.3 MEASURES TO PROMOTE NATIONAL INTEGRATION

(1) CONSTITUTIONAL MEASURES
 - SINGLE CITIZENSHIP (Article 5).
 - UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE.
 - PROHIBITION OF DISCRIMINATION on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15).
 - ABOLITION OF UNTOUCHABILITY (Article 17).
 - FREEDOM OF MOVEMENT and RESIDENCE throughout India (Article 19).
 - SECULAR state (Preamble).
 - FUNDAMENTAL DUTY (Article 51A(e)) to promote harmony.

(2) POLITICAL MEASURES
 - Reorganisation of states on a LINGUISTIC basis (States Reorganisation Act 1956) — gave linguistic minorities their own states, reducing tensions.
 - Provision for special protection of tribal and culturally distinct areas (Sixth Schedule for NE; Article 371 special provisions for various states).
 - Federal structure that respects regional autonomy.
 - Political INCLUSION of all communities in government.

(3) EDUCATIONAL MEASURES
 - Teaching of NATIONAL HISTORY emphasising shared heritage.
 - PROMOTION of major Indian languages — three-language formula in schools.
 - CIVIC EDUCATION on Constitution, fundamental rights and duties.
 - INTER-FAITH dialogue and curriculum sensitivity.

(4) ECONOMIC MEASURES
 - Balanced regional development through Five-Year Plans and centrally sponsored schemes.
 - Special programmes for backward areas (Aspirational Districts), tribal areas, NE region (Look East / Act East Policy).
 - Public sector industries in less-developed states.

(5) SOCIAL AND CULTURAL MEASURES
 - Celebration of NATIONAL FESTIVALS (Republic Day, Independence Day, Gandhi Jayanti) bringing all communities together.
 - REPUBLIC DAY PARADE showcases unity in diversity (different state tableaux, military pageantry).
 - National symbols — the FLAG (Tiranga), ANTHEM (Jana Gana Mana), SONG (Vande Mataram), EMBLEM (Lion Capital of Sarnath).
 - Sports — cricket, hockey — bring Indians together regardless of region.
 - Hindi cinema (Bollywood) and regional cinema cross-pollinate.
 - National Integration Council (constituted by PM Nehru in 1961) brings together leaders to promote integration.

24.4 SECULARISM — THE INDIAN MEANING

Indian secularism is a distinctive concept. Unlike WESTERN SECULARISM (a strict wall of separation between state and religion), INDIAN SECULARISM is based on:

(1) EQUAL RESPECT FOR ALL RELIGIONS (sarva dharma sambhava).
(2) NO OFFICIAL STATE RELIGION.
(3) FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE and worship for every citizen (Articles 25-28).
(4) Equal CITIZENSHIP regardless of religion (Articles 14, 15).
(5) STATE INTERVENTION in religious affairs only to PROTECT FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS or REFORM unjust practices (e.g. abolition of untouchability, ban on child marriage, opening temples to all castes).
(6) AID and protection for minority religious institutions (Articles 29-30).

The word 'SECULAR' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), but the Constitution was always secular in spirit. The Supreme Court has held SECULARISM to be part of the BASIC STRUCTURE of the Constitution — it cannot be amended away.

24.5 CHALLENGES TO SECULARISM

 - Use of religious appeals in elections (despite legal prohibition).
 - Communal violence (riots, hate crimes, mob lynching).
 - HATE SPEECH and propaganda by political and religious leaders.
 - DISCRIMINATION in jobs, housing, business based on religion.
 - Religious vote-banks distorting policy.
 - Religious organisations claiming the right to impose their views on others.

24.6 PROTECTING SECULARISM

 - Strict enforcement of CONSTITUTIONAL provisions (Articles 25-28, 15, 17).
 - PROSECUTION of hate speech and communal violence.
 - INTER-FAITH DIALOGUE and joint celebrations.
 - CIVIC EDUCATION emphasising secular values.
 - MEDIA responsibility — not sensationalising religious incidents.
 - Personal CONDUCT — every citizen practising respect for all faiths.
 - JUDICIAL ACTIVISM upholding secular values.

SUMMARY

- India is one of the most diverse countries in the world — religions, languages, castes, regions.
- NATIONAL INTEGRATION is the feeling of oneness as Indian citizens, transcending differences — 'unity in diversity'.
- Obstacles include communalism, casteism, regionalism, linguistic tensions, economic disparities, separatist movements.
- Constitutional, political, educational, economic and cultural measures promote integration.
- SECULARISM is the Indian state's principled distance from all religions — equal respect, no official religion, freedom of conscience for all.
- Indian secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution; it requires the active commitment of every citizen.

chapter_summary.title: National Integration and Secularism — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 24 explains how India, one of the most diverse countries in the world, holds together as a nation. NATIONAL INTEGRATION is the feeling of oneness among all Indian citizens transcending differences of religion, caste, language and region — 'unity in diversity'. SECULARISM is the constitutional principle of equal respect for all religions and principled distance of the state from any religion. Together they are essential to the Indian Republic.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — National Integration and Secularism
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use specific examples and constitutional articles where possible.

questions.question: Define 'national integration'. Why is the phrase 'unity in diversity' often used in connection with India?
questions.answer:
NATIONAL INTEGRATION is the feeling of ONENESS among all citizens of a country, transcending differences of religion, caste, language and region. It is the recognition that despite our many differences, we share a common political and emotional bond as ONE NATION.

The phrase 'UNITY IN DIVERSITY' is used for India because: (1) India contains an enormous variety of religions, languages, castes, tribes, foods, costumes, festivals — perhaps more diversity than any other country. (2) Yet Indians share a common political identity, a common Constitution, a common stake in the nation's future. (3) Indian civilisation has historically absorbed and integrated different cultures — Aryan, Dravidian, Persian, Arab, Mongol, European — without obliterating them. India's strength is that it has built unity WHILE PRESERVING diversity, rather than by imposing uniformity. This is the essence of 'unity in diversity'.

questions.question: State five obstacles to national integration in India.
questions.answer:
(1) COMMUNALISM — religion-based politics and violence (e.g. Partition, Gujarat 2002).
(2) CASTEISM — caste-based discrimination and atrocities.
(3) REGIONALISM — anti-migrant 'sons-of-soil' violence, separatist demands, inter-state disputes.
(4) LINGUISTIC TENSIONS — disputes over Hindi imposition, demands for new states.
(5) ECONOMIC DISPARITIES — uneven development between rich and poor states, tribal areas left behind.
(6) SEPARATIST MOVEMENTS — historical agitations in Punjab, J&K, the North-east; Left-Wing Extremism.
(7) EXTERNAL FORCES — neighbouring countries that may support insurgents and terrorists.

questions.question: List five constitutional measures that promote national integration.
questions.answer:
(1) SINGLE CITIZENSHIP (Article 5) — every Indian is a citizen of India, not of any state.
(2) UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE — every citizen 18+ has the right to vote regardless of caste, religion, sex.
(3) PROHIBITION OF DISCRIMINATION on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth (Article 15).
(4) ABOLITION OF UNTOUCHABILITY (Article 17).
(5) FREEDOM OF MOVEMENT and RESIDENCE throughout India (Article 19).
(6) SECULAR state (Preamble + Articles 25-28).
(7) FUNDAMENTAL DUTY (Article 51A(e)) to promote HARMONY and common brotherhood across diversity.
(8) Provisions for special protection of tribal and culturally distinct areas (Sixth Schedule, Article 371).

questions.question: How did the States Reorganisation Act 1956 help reduce regional tensions?
questions.answer:
After independence, India was a federation of 28 states and many princely-state territories formed mainly for administrative convenience under the British. Many regions wanted their own state defined by LANGUAGE — feeling that they could only protect their culture and have effective government if administered in their own language. Agitations broke out — most dramatically, Potti Sriramulu's death after a fast for a separate Andhra Pradesh in 1952.

The FAZL ALI Commission (1953) recommended reorganisation on linguistic lines. The STATES REORGANISATION ACT 1956 redrew India into 14 states and 6 union territories, broadly along linguistic lines — Andhra (Telugu), Karnataka (Kannada), Kerala (Malayalam), Tamil Nadu (Tamil), Maharashtra (Marathi later), Gujarat (Gujarati later), etc.

This REDUCED regional tensions by: (1) giving each major linguistic community its own state with administration in its own language; (2) removing one major source of grievance; (3) facilitating better education and governance; (4) demonstrating that India would accommodate diversity within unity. Later, more states were created (Punjab/Haryana 1966, Northeast states, Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh/Uttarakhand 2000, Telangana 2014).

questions.question: Define 'secularism' as it is understood in the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer:
In the Indian Constitution, secularism means:
(1) The state has NO OFFICIAL RELIGION.
(2) The state TREATS ALL RELIGIONS WITH EQUAL RESPECT (sarva dharma sambhava) — neither favouring nor discriminating against any religion.
(3) Every CITIZEN has the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion (Articles 25-28).
(4) Religion cannot be a ground for discrimination in citizenship, employment, education or any sphere of public life (Articles 14, 15, 16).
(5) The state CAN intervene in religious matters to REFORM unjust practices (e.g. abolition of untouchability, prohibition of child marriage) or to protect fundamental rights.
(6) Religious and linguistic minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions (Articles 29-30).

The word 'SECULAR' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, but the Constitution was always secular in spirit. The Supreme Court has held SECULARISM to be part of the BASIC STRUCTURE — it cannot be amended away.

questions.question: Compare Indian secularism with western (American or French) secularism.
questions.answer:
WESTERN SECULARISM (US, France) is based on a STRICT SEPARATION between state and religion — a 'WALL OF SEPARATION'. The state stays out of religious affairs; religious institutions stay out of public life. The French principle of LAÏCITÉ keeps religious symbols out of public schools and offices; the US First Amendment forbids the establishment of any religion.

INDIAN SECULARISM, by contrast, is based on PRINCIPLED DISTANCE and EQUAL RESPECT (sarva dharma sambhava). It has these distinctive features:
 - The state has no official religion but RESPECTS ALL religions equally.
 - The state may ENGAGE WITH religious institutions — by providing aid to minority schools (Article 30), recognising religious personal laws, regulating temple management.
 - The state may INTERVENE in religious matters to REFORM unjust practices — abolish untouchability, ban child marriage, open temples to all castes.
 - There is no strict ban on religious symbols in public — Indian leaders openly visit temples, mosques, churches.

Why India chose this: India is a DEEPLY RELIGIOUS SOCIETY with multiple faiths. A strict western-style separation was neither possible nor desirable. The Indian model preserves religious freedom while allowing the state to ensure equal citizenship and reform unjust practices. It is sometimes called 'POSITIVE SECULARISM' or 'CONTEXTUAL SECULARISM'.

questions.question: Name the constitutional articles that protect freedom of religion.
questions.answer:
Articles 25-28 collectively protect freedom of religion:
 - ARTICLE 25 — Freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise and propagate religion (subject to public order, morality, health).
 - ARTICLE 26 — Freedom to manage religious affairs (establish institutions, own property, administer them).
 - ARTICLE 27 — No person can be compelled to pay any tax for the promotion of any particular religion.
 - ARTICLE 28 — No religious instruction in state-funded educational institutions.

Additionally, Articles 29-30 protect the language, culture and educational rights of religious and linguistic minorities — and Articles 14-15 prohibit discrimination on religious grounds.

questions.question: What role do national symbols play in fostering integration?
questions.answer:
NATIONAL SYMBOLS are powerful tools of national integration because they belong to ALL Indians regardless of religion, caste, language or region.

Major symbols:
 - NATIONAL FLAG (Tiranga) — horizontal bands of saffron, white and green with the Ashoka Chakra in the centre. Adopted 22 July 1947.
 - NATIONAL ANTHEM — 'Jana Gana Mana', composed by Rabindranath Tagore; adopted 24 January 1950.
 - NATIONAL SONG — 'Vande Mataram', from Bankim Chandra's Anandamath.
 - NATIONAL EMBLEM — adaptation of the Lion Capital of Sarnath (Ashoka's pillar), with the motto SATYAMEVA JAYATE ('truth alone triumphs').
 - NATIONAL ANIMAL — Tiger (since 1973); previously Lion.
 - NATIONAL BIRD — Peacock.
 - NATIONAL FLOWER — Lotus.
 - NATIONAL FRUIT — Mango.
 - NATIONAL TREE — Banyan.

When citizens salute the FLAG, sing the ANTHEM, celebrate REPUBLIC DAY and INDEPENDENCE DAY, they share a moment of common Indian identity that transcends the differences of daily life. National symbols are also taught from childhood, embedding the sense of shared belonging.

questions.question: What can ordinary citizens do to promote national integration?
questions.answer:
Citizens can take many small but important steps:
(1) RESPECT all religions, languages, castes, regions — practise the spirit of sarva dharma sambhava.
(2) Be careful with WORDS — avoid stereotypes, slurs and hate speech.
(3) BUILD FRIENDSHIPS across community lines — colleagues, neighbours, schoolmates.
(4) PARTICIPATE in inter-community festivals — wishing neighbours on their festivals; joining mohalla peace committees.
(5) RESIST RUMOURS — verify before forwarding messages; refuse to amplify communal hate.
(6) STAND UP against discrimination or violence — defend the vulnerable.
(7) FULFIL FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES — especially Article 51A(e) on promoting harmony.
(8) LEARN about other communities, religions, regional cultures.
(9) SUPPORT INSTITUTIONS that build integration — schools, NGOs, civil society.
(10) VOTE for candidates who unify, not divide.
Every act of friendship across community lines builds the nation. Every act of bigotry or violence tears it down.

questions.question: What constitutional and legal mechanisms protect secularism?
questions.answer:
CONSTITUTIONAL:
 - PREAMBLE — declares India a SECULAR republic.
 - ARTICLES 14, 15 — equality before law; prohibition of discrimination on religious grounds.
 - ARTICLE 17 — abolishes untouchability.
 - ARTICLES 25-28 — freedom of religion.
 - ARTICLES 29-30 — minority cultural and educational rights.
 - ARTICLE 51A(e) — fundamental duty to promote harmony.
 - Basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati) — secularism cannot be amended away.

LEGAL:
 - SECTIONS 153A and 295A of the Indian Penal Code — criminalise hate speech, deliberate insult of religious feelings.
 - REPRESENTATION OF PEOPLE ACT 1951 — prohibits religious appeals in election campaigns; corrupt practice.
 - UNLAWFUL ACTIVITIES (PREVENTION) ACT — to ban communal organisations.
 - PROTECTION OF CIVIL RIGHTS ACT 1955 — enforces Article 17 against untouchability.
 - SC/ST (PREVENTION OF ATROCITIES) ACT 1989 — protects against caste-based violence.

INSTITUTIONAL:
 - NHRC, Minorities Commission, SC/ST Commission monitor and report violations.
 - JUDICIARY actively reviews laws and government actions that may violate secularism.
 - ELECTION COMMISSION enforces the model code of conduct.

questions.question: Write an essay on the importance of national integration and secularism for India's future.
questions.answer:
India's future depends on NATIONAL INTEGRATION and SECULARISM. These are not luxuries but necessities.

WHY INTEGRATION MATTERS: India is one of the most diverse countries in the world. Without a shared sense of being Indian, this diversity could fracture — as Partition showed. Development requires internal peace and free movement; communal violence paralyses investment. Democracy needs citizens who can debate, disagree, and still see each other as fellow members of one polity. National security requires that internal divisions are not exploited by external enemies. India's global standing as a model of pluralism rests on a successful diverse democracy.

WHY SECULARISM MATTERS: In a country of hundreds of religious communities, secularism is the only fair way for the state to relate to its citizens. Privileging one religion would make others second-class. Indian secularism combines respect for religion with reform of unjust practices — allowing continuity with civilisational heritage even as we abolish untouchability. Secularism is the foundation of equal citizenship — no Indian should be denied a job, school or public office because of religion. In times of communal tension, the constitutional commitment to secularism lets the state act fairly.

THE FUTURE: Urbanisation, social-media polarisation, inequality and external pressures will continue to test both values. The response must be constant — firm enforcement of law, civic education, inter-community dialogue, balanced development, responsible media, and personal commitment from every citizen. Today's students will build tomorrow's India. Whether it remains one nation under the Constitution depends on whether these values remain alive in citizens' hearts.

The Constitution gives the framework. The rest is up to us.

questions.explanation: Different communities sharing a common Indian identity.

questions.explanation: Up from 14; expanded by 92nd Amendment in 2003.

questions.explanation: After the Fazl Ali Commission report.

questions.question: The National Integration Council was first constituted by PM ____.
The Sanskrit phrase for 'equal respect for all religions' is ____ ____ sambhava.
The word 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the ____ Amendment.
India's national anthem ____ was composed by Rabindranath Tagore.
India's national song, ____ , was composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay.
The motto on India's national emblem is ____ Jayate.
India's national animal is the ____.

Freedom of religion is guaranteed by Articles 25 to ____.

The French principle of strict separation between state and religion is called ____.
The Supreme Court has held that secularism is part of the ____ structure of the Constitution.
The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution applies to certain ____ areas in the Northeast.
Why is India called one of the most diverse countries in the world?
questions.answer: Because of the sheer variety of: (1) RELIGIONS — Hindus (~80%), Muslims (~14%), Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Zoroastrians, Jews, plus many tribal religions. (2) LANGUAGES — 22 scheduled languages, hundreds of others spoken; the Indian Census records over 19,500 mother tongues. (3) CASTES AND TRIBES — thousands of castes (jatis) and over 700 Scheduled Tribes. (4) GEOGRAPHY AND CLIMATE — from snowy Himalayas to tropical beaches, deserts to rainforests. (5) FOOD, DRESS, FESTIVALS, ARTS, MUSIC — distinctive regional traditions across the country. Despite all this diversity, India is held together by a common Constitution, democracy, currency, and citizenship — a remarkable achievement.

questions.question: How does economic disparity threaten national integration?
questions.answer:
Several ways: (1) UNEVEN DEVELOPMENT between states creates resentment — poorer states (Bihar, Odisha, UP) feel left behind compared to richer ones (Punjab, Haryana, Maharashtra, Karnataka). (2) MIGRATION from poor states to richer ones triggers 'sons-of-soil' tensions and anti-migrant violence. (3) TRIBAL AREAS that have been bypassed by development have been receptive to LEFT-WING EXTREMISM. (4) Regional ECONOMIC GRIEVANCES feed separatist movements (NE states, Punjab in 1980s). (5) Resource disputes (water, minerals) between states sharpen interstate hostility. (6) Cross-border ECONOMIC GAPS — when an Indian state is much poorer than its neighbour in another country, populations there can feel cheated.

Remedies: BALANCED DEVELOPMENT through Finance Commission transfers; centrally sponsored schemes targeting backward areas (Aspirational Districts); Look East / Act East policy for NE; cooperative federalism; investment in tribal regions.

questions.question: What is the three-language formula and why was it adopted?
questions.answer:
The THREE-LANGUAGE FORMULA is the educational policy adopted in the National Education Policy of 1968 (and continued in later policies). It says that every Indian student should learn THREE languages in school:
 - In NON-HINDI states: the MOTHER TONGUE (regional language), HINDI, and ENGLISH.
 - In HINDI-speaking states: the MOTHER TONGUE (Hindi), ENGLISH, and a MODERN INDIAN LANGUAGE from a non-Hindi region.

WHY IT WAS ADOPTED:
(1) To preserve the MOTHER TONGUE and the rich linguistic diversity of India.
(2) To promote HINDI as a link language to facilitate national integration.
(3) To retain ENGLISH for higher education, science, technology and international communication.
(4) To create UNDERSTANDING ACROSS REGIONS — Hindi speakers learn a southern language; non-Hindi speakers learn Hindi; everyone gets English.
(5) To AVOID IMPOSITION of any single language on unwilling regions (especially after the anti-Hindi protests in Tamil Nadu in 1965).

In practice, implementation has been uneven — many Hindi-belt schools do not teach a southern language; some southern states (esp. Tamil Nadu) follow a two-language formula (Tamil + English).

questions.question: State the constitutional provisions that protect minority rights in India.
questions.answer:
(1) ARTICLE 15 — Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
(2) ARTICLE 16 — Equality of opportunity in public employment, including for religious minorities.
(3) ARTICLES 25-28 — Freedom of religion: profess, practise, propagate; manage religious affairs; no religious tax; no religious instruction in state-funded schools.
(4) ARTICLE 29 — Protection of language, script and culture of minorities; no denial of admission to state-aided educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.
(5) ARTICLE 30 — Right of RELIGIOUS AND LINGUISTIC MINORITIES to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice; state must not discriminate in granting aid.
(6) NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR MINORITIES — statutory body monitoring minority rights.
(7) STATE Minority Commissions in many states.

questions.question: In what sense can Indian secularism be called 'positive' or 'engaged'?
questions.answer:
Indian secularism is called 'POSITIVE' or 'ENGAGED' because, unlike the western model of strict separation, the Indian state ACTIVELY ENGAGES with religion in specific ways to ensure equal citizenship and reform unjust practices:

(1) EQUAL RESPECT — The state celebrates the festivals and recognises the holidays of all major religions, not just one.
(2) AID TO MINORITY INSTITUTIONS — The state may give grants to minority schools (Article 30), enabling them to flourish.
(3) REFORM OF UNJUST PRACTICES — The state has acted against TRIPLE TALAQ, SATI, CHILD MARRIAGE, UNTOUCHABILITY, dowry — all matters intimately tied to religion or religious tradition.
(4) OPENING TEMPLES to all castes (Article 25(2)(b)) — Hindu temples cannot exclude Dalits or other backward classes.
(5) Personal laws are recognised (Hindu, Muslim, Christian) but the state can REGULATE them where they conflict with fundamental rights.
(6) Religious leaders' MISCONDUCT can be punished — the state does not give religious immunity to violations of secular law.

This 'engaged' secularism is suited to India's deeply religious society, where ignoring religion would not work. It tries to BALANCE respect for religion with the constitutional demands of equality and dignity. It is not always easy and is sometimes controversial — but it is distinctively Indian.

questions.question: What is the role of the judiciary in protecting secularism?
questions.answer:
The Indian judiciary, especially the Supreme Court, has played a major role in protecting secularism:
(1) BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE (Kesavananda Bharati 1973 and subsequent cases) — held that SECULARISM is part of the basic structure of the Constitution and CANNOT be amended away.
(2) STRIKING DOWN of laws and government actions that violate secular principles.
(3) RULING on disputes involving religion — e.g. the Ayodhya verdict (2019), Sabarimala (2018), Triple Talaq (2017), Same-Sex Marriage (2023).
(4) RESTRAINING religious appeals in elections — held them to be a corrupt practice under the Representation of People Act.
(5) HATE SPEECH cases — ruling that hate speech is not protected by free speech.
(6) REVIEWING action / inaction of the state in communal incidents (e.g. 2002 Gujarat riots cases).
(7) PUBLIC INTEREST LITIGATION (PIL) — allows ordinary citizens to bring secular violations to court.

The judiciary acts as the LAST LINE OF DEFENCE when political institutions fail. Its independence and its commitment to constitutional values are critical to keeping Indian secularism alive.

questions.question: How do sports and cinema contribute to national integration?
questions.answer:
SPORTS:
 - When the Indian cricket, hockey or football team plays, all Indians — regardless of religion, caste, language — cheer together. The team itself is a microcosm of India's diversity.
 - Stars like Sachin Tendulkar (Maharashtra), M.S. Dhoni (Jharkhand), Virat Kohli (Delhi), Rohit Sharma (Mumbai), Hardik Pandya (Gujarat), Ravichandran Ashwin (Tamil Nadu), Rishabh Pant (Uttarakhand), Bumrah (Gujarat), Mary Kom (Manipur), P.V. Sindhu (Andhra), Neeraj Chopra (Haryana) are loved across regions.
 - National team selection brings people from all backgrounds together.
 - The OLYMPIC representation of India unites the country in common pride.

CINEMA:
 - INDIAN CINEMA (Hindi 'Bollywood' + regional Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Bengali, Marathi, Punjabi) is consumed across the country and abroad — building a shared cultural vocabulary.
 - Films often portray characters from different religions, regions, languages — normalising diversity.
 - Songs and stars cross regional barriers — a Tamil film like Baahubali becomes a national hit.
 - Themes of religious harmony, national pride, and shared history are recurrent.
 - National film awards and the Bharat Ratna for great artistes celebrate Indian creative talent regardless of region.

Both sports and cinema create EMOTIONAL BONDS across diversity that policy and law alone cannot.

questions.question: What does Article 25 of the Constitution guarantee?
questions.answer:
Article 25(1) states: 'Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE and the right freely to PROFESS, PRACTISE AND PROPAGATE religion.'

It has four elements: (1) FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE — the inner freedom to choose one's beliefs. (2) Right to PROFESS — publicly declare one's religion. (3) Right to PRACTISE — perform religious rites, worship, follow rules. (4) Right to PROPAGATE — share one's faith with others (subject to others' freedom).

This right is subject to: PUBLIC ORDER, MORALITY, HEALTH and the other Fundamental Rights. So religious practices that harm others or violate fundamental rights (e.g. untouchability, denial of temple entry to certain castes) are NOT protected. Article 25(2) explicitly allows the state to: regulate secular activities associated with religious practice; provide for SOCIAL WELFARE AND REFORM, including the opening of Hindu religious institutions to all classes of Hindus.

questions.question: Give five practical things a young Indian can do to promote secularism in daily life.
questions.answer:
(1) BE FRIENDS with people of other religions — visit their homes, eat their food, attend their celebrations.
(2) CELEBRATE FESTIVALS together — wish your neighbours on Eid, Christmas, Diwali, Guru Purab, Buddha Purnima.
(3) RESIST HATE FORWARDS — verify before sharing news or messages that target any religious group; refuse to amplify hate content on social media.
(4) SPEAK UP gently when you hear religious slurs, stereotypes or jokes — even within your own family or friend group.
(5) LEARN about other religions — read their basic texts, understand their festivals, visit places of worship as a respectful visitor.
(6) STAND WITH the vulnerable — if someone is being harassed because of their religion (in public transport, at work, online), offer support.
(7) VOTE for candidates who unify rather than divide.
(8) ENGAGE with diverse co-workers, classmates, neighbours — break the bubble of monoreligious interactions.
(9) Where possible, READ AUTHORS and watch films from different communities; the imagination must be plural.
(10) Bring up CHILDREN with respect for all religions — secularism starts at home.

Every small act of cross-community friendship strengthens India. Every act of bigotry weakens it.

questions.question: Why is the Indian model of secularism not a 'strict wall of separation' between state and religion?
questions.answer: Because Indian society is deeply RELIGIOUS — for most Indians, religion is woven into daily life, family, festivals, ethics. A strict separation as in France or the US was neither possible nor desirable. Several factors shaped India's distinctive model: (1) HISTORICAL — Indian civilisation has long traditions of religious coexistence (Ashoka, Akbar). (2) PRACTICAL — religious institutions (temples, mosques, gurdwaras, churches) play huge social roles in education, charity, festivals. (3) JUSTICE — the state must INTERVENE in religion to reform unjust practices like untouchability and child marriage; pure separation would have left these unaddressed. (4) PROTECTION OF MINORITIES — the state must positively support minority cultural and educational institutions through aid (Article 30). So Indian secularism is one of EQUAL RESPECT and PRINCIPLED ENGAGEMENT, not strict separation.

questions.question: What can be done to address each of the main obstacles to national integration?
questions.answer:
COMMUNALISM: enforce IPC sections against hate speech; ban religious appeals in elections; prosecute riot perpetrators; promote inter-faith dialogue; teach shared history; responsible media reporting.

CASTEISM: enforce Article 17 and SC/ST Atrocities Act; fast-track caste-violence cases; reservations in education, jobs, legislatures to address historical disadvantage; encourage inter-caste interaction and marriage; build economic mobility to weaken caste-based hierarchies.

REGIONALISM: cooperative federalism; balanced regional development; respect for linguistic and cultural diversity; quick redress of inter-state disputes; protection of internal migration under Article 19; firm action against anti-migrant violence; engaging youth in national service.

LINGUISTIC TENSIONS: implement the three-language formula meaningfully (so that Hindi-belt students learn a southern language too); resist imposition of any language; promote translations across languages; recognise regional languages in their domains.

ECONOMIC DISPARITIES: targeted development of backward regions (Aspirational Districts); special focus on NE (Act East), tribal areas; transparent Finance Commission transfers; investment in education, health, infrastructure in lagging states.

SEPARATIST MOVEMENTS: combination of security action, political dialogue, and economic development (the model that worked in Punjab and parts of NE); generous accommodation of legitimate cultural/political demands; rejection of violence; bringing former militants into mainstream politics.

EXTERNAL FORCES: diplomacy with neighbours; intelligence cooperation; sealing of borders against infiltration; military preparedness; addressing internal grievances so they cannot be exploited.

The overarching strategy is: BUILD STAKES for every Indian in the success of the Indian project, so that no one finds it more attractive to break away than to belong.
